content: The MT-TT gene, also known as mitochondrially encoded tRNA threonine, is a transfer RNA gene located in human mitochondrial DNA. It is specifically situated on the p arm of mitochondrial DNA at position 12 and spans 66 base pairs. The structure of the tRNA encoded by MT-TT is characterized by a unique folded configuration that includes three hairpin loops, giving it a cloverleaf-like appearance. The MT-TT gene encodes a small RNA molecule consisting of 66 nucleotides, corresponding to the mitochondrial map position 15888-15953. This RNA plays a critical role in protein synthesis by transferring the amino acid threonine to the growing polypeptide chain at the ribosome during the process of translation. Mutations in the MT-TT gene have been implicated in several mitochondrial disorders, including myoclonic epilepsy with ragged-red fibers (MERRF). MERRF is a rare mitochondrial disease that primarily affects the muscles and nervous system. Symptoms of MERRF typically manifest during childhood or adolescence, although the clinical presentation can vary significantly even among individuals within the same family. Common symptoms include myoclonus (involuntary muscle jerks), muscle weakness (myopathy), spasticity, epilepsy, peripheral neuropathy, dementia, ataxia (loss of coordination), and muscle atrophy. Additionally, MT-TT mutations have been associated with other conditions, such as lethal infantile mitochondrial myopathy, Parkinson's disease linked to the 15950G>A mutation, and a 15923A>G mutation that has been tentatively associated with heart disease. MT-TT mutations are also known to cause cytochrome c oxidase deficiency, a condition resulting from a defect in complex IV of the mitochondrial respiratory chain. Cytochrome c oxidase deficiency is a rare genetic disorder that can affect various organs, including skeletal muscles, the heart, the brain, and the liver. Clinical manifestations of this condition often include muscle weakness (myopathy), low muscle tone (hypotonia), encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis, and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. A specific mutation, 15915G>A, has been identified in a patient with cytochrome c oxidase deficiency, who presented with symptoms such as seizures, progressive hearing loss, and muscle weakness.
